summary: A report of an IAB workshop held in March 1997 at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, New Jersey. Participants identified the core security components of the Internet architecture, listed documents that needed to be written, and agreed that security must not be optional.

plainLanguage.summary: A group of experts met for three days and agreed that internet safety is not an extra feature but a must, and made a to-do list for it.

questions: what was the iab security architecture workshop
why did the iab say security is not optional
what are core security protocols in rfc 2316
subtitle: A 1997 workshop report that argued security must be designed in, not bolted on.

tldr.problem: Internet attacks were increasing and many protocols had security sections that said little or nothing, so the IAB wanted a security architecture and guidance for protocol designers.
tldr.mechanism: Twenty-four attendees met at Bell Labs on 3-5 March 1997, picked core security protocols, named missing pieces, listed documents to write and drafted guidelines for Security Considerations sections.
tldr.outcome: The report is Informational. Its main conclusion is that security is not optional and must be designed in from the beginning.

today: RFC 2316 is an Informational workshop report from April 1998, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records the views of one workshop, not an Internet standard.

sections.title: Why the IAB Held the Workshop
sections.content:
The IAB held the workshop on 3-5 March 1997 at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, NJ. The goal was a security architecture for the Internet: to understand which security tools exist, where each is useful and where adequate tools are missing, and to give protocol designers guidance. The aim was to be able to stop RFCs from saying security issues are not discussed in this memo.

The report describes a worsening situation. Canned exploit scripts were common, attackers were more and more often targeting infrastructure such as routers and high-level name servers, and users and administrators wanted magic security regardless of whether it was real.
sections.plainLanguage: Break-ins were getting easier and more common, so the experts met to figure out how to build better locks.

sections.title: Philosophy and the IETF's Structure
sections.content:
The group concluded that end-to-end security is generally better. For email, one should use something like PGP or S/MIME rather than rely on an IPsec layer, because relying on the infrastructure is a bad idea. At best the infrastructure should provide availability.

The report also admits an organizational problem. The IETF is a volunteer organization, so it is unclear who should do security work and whether the IESG can impose new requirements on existing working groups. It warns that IPsec will not solve everything: it protects packets in transit but is hard to deploy on individual hosts, does not protect objects that may be retransmitted such as email, does not address authorization and cannot block excess resource consumption.
sections.plainLanguage: Locking only the road is not enough, so each message should carry its own lock. And a volunteer club cannot easily force its members to add locks.

sections.title: Guidelines for Security Considerations
sections.content:
A threat is defined as a vulnerability available to a motivated and capable adversary. The report recommends that all RFCs MUST meaningfully address security and MUST do due diligence in listing the threats the protocol is vulnerable to.

For each threat the RFC MUST say whether it is ameliorated by protocol mechanisms, ameliorated by reliance on external mechanisms, irrelevant, or not addressed by the protocol. In the last case the result is an applicability statement, such as saying the protocol should not be used in an environment subject to that attack.

It also proposes charter text under which protocols are analyzed for security breaches, and identified threats are removed if possible or documented and guarded against.
sections.plainLanguage: Every new protocol has to write down how it could be attacked and what it does about each attack, not just say nothing.

sections.title: Core Mechanisms and Missing Pieces
sections.content:
The workshop designated core protocols to prefer when their properties fit: IPsec (RFC 1825) with HMAC (RFC 2104), ISAKMP/Oakley for key negotiation, DNSsec (RFC 2065), Security/Multipart (RFC 1847), signed keys in the DNS, X.509v3 and TLS. For the last three the report says there was no strong consensus.

Others were useful but not core, and PEM and MOSS were called not useful because they failed to catch on. One mechanism was deemed unacceptable: plaintext passwords sent over unencrypted channels.

Three pieces were missing: object security, secure email and route security. For route security the report notes that the demand for maximum router performance conflicts with adding security.
sections.plainLanguage: They made a short list of trusted tools, a list of maybe tools, and one firm rule: never send a password in the open.

sections.title: Documents to Write and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The workshop decided on several documents: a taxonomy of attacks, implementation hints and pitfalls, firewall issues, and the workshop report itself. Firewalls are described as both a common defense and a much-reviled wart that is unlikely to go away soon.

The report's own Security Considerations says that security is not a cookie cutter process and there is no magic pixie dust. Each protocol must be analyzed individually for its vulnerabilities, the risks they lead to, the palliative measures available and the residual risks.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no one spell that makes everything safe. Each thing you build has to be checked on its own.

viz.caption: THREE MISSING PIECES NAMED BY THE WORKSHOP

items.title: Object security
items.text: Protection for individual data objects, independent of transport.

items.title: Secure email
items.text: A critical need for some time; PEM and MOSS were not accepted.

items.title: Route security
items.text: Needed because attacks on routing were rising, but it competes with router performance.
